vignette:
Rohan stepped out of his truck at the trailhead and felt the familiar knot tighten in his chest. A state trooper’s cruiser was parked near the map kiosk, and as Rohan walked past, he caught a glimpse of the officer in his dark blue uniform standing beside the vehicle. The sight of that crisp shirt, the badge, the heavy belt—it was nothing like the mismatched fatigues of the militia, but his body did not know the difference. His breath shortened, his palms went cold, and he had to force himself to keep moving toward the maintenance shed. He told himself he needed to check the chainsaw fuel, but the real reason was simpler: he could not bear to be near anyone in a uniform, because that shape meant someone who could decide whether he lived or died.

Thirteen years earlier, when Rohan was twenty-eight, he had been part of a small conservation team working in a remote region of Southeast Asia. They had been taken by a militia group that wore mismatched fatigues and carried automatic weapons. For six weeks, Rohan was kept in a concrete room with no windows. He was beaten across his ribs and the backs of his legs whenever he failed to answer a question correctly—the questions changed each time, so he never knew what the right answer was. The worst part was the unpredictability: one guard would bring him water, the next would kick him in the same spot. He learned to watch for the smallest change in a person’s posture or tone, because that flicker of movement meant something was about to happen.

Now, at forty-one and working as a park ranger in a quiet state forest, Rohan’s body still reacted as if the danger had never stopped. An unexpected movement in his peripheral vision—a deer jumping across the trail, a child darting behind a picnic table—would send a jolt through his whole frame, his hands flying up before his mind could catch up. But there were also moments when the past completely overtook him. Once, while refueling a chainsaw near the maintenance shed, a generator sputtered and coughed to life behind him. The sound—the exact pitch and rhythm of the generator that had run day and night outside his prison—sent him crashing to the ground, his hands covering his head, his body curled into a tight ball. For several seconds he was not in the forest; he was back in that concrete room, expecting the next kick. He came to with a fellow ranger kneeling beside him, asking if he was okay, and the shame of being seen like that—cowering, helpless—burned in his throat. He made an excuse about tripping over a root, but he avoided that ranger for weeks.

The memory itself came in fragments. He could recall the guard’s boots, the crack in the ceiling, the sound of a generator starting—each moment a frozen snapshot, isolated from the others. Sometimes, when the memory surfaced, he felt a sharp pain in his ribs and the backs of his legs, as if the bruises were fresh. Other times, he could describe the entire six weeks to his girlfriend, Sarah, in a flat, detached voice, feeling nothing at all, as though he were narrating someone else’s life. That numbness frightened him more than the pain.

To manage the constant sense of impending threat, Rohan had developed a strict set of invisible rules. He controlled his eating with military precision: exactly two meals a day, the same portion size, no snacks. If he lost control of that, he reasoned, everything else would follow. When he was around other people—fellow rangers, hikers, even Sarah—he said yes to whatever they wanted, agreed with whatever plan they proposed, because disagreeing had once meant punishment. He kept his head down and his voice soft. But being watched was unbearable. In the visitor center, he always positioned himself so his back was to the wall and he could see every entrance. If a hiker lingered too long near his desk, or if he caught someone’s eyes on him through the window, his skin would prickle and his concentration would shatter. And whenever he spotted a person in uniform—a police officer checking a permit, a firefighter passing through, even a security guard at a nearby reservoir—his mind would seize on a single thought: this person can do anything to me, and I will not be able to stop it. He had come to believe that attention was dangerous—that if someone observed him closely, they would discover how weak he really was. Alone in his truck, or lying awake at three in the morning, he allowed himself the full, bitter pleasure of revenge fantasies. He imagined the faces of the three men who had interrogated him; he imagined what he would do to them if the roles were reversed. The fantasy gave him a feeling of power that he never felt in his actual life.

Military topics were a separate but equally sharp trigger. Over lunch in the ranger station, a colleague once mentioned a news segment about a peacekeeping deployment in the Middle East, and Rohan felt his chest lock. The words military exercise from another ranger describing his son’s ROTC program made Rohan’s jaw clench—he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he stood over the sink, gripping the porcelain, waiting for the images of armed men shouting orders to fade. Sarah had stopped bringing up military-themed movies or podcasts after the first time, when Rohan went silent and then snapped at her for no reason. He could not explain that any talk of armies, soldiers, or armed groups—even in a benign context—dragged him back to his captors’ voices, the crackle of their radios, the casual brutality of their commands.

Those triggers were the only time he did not feel isolated. At work, he watched his colleagues joke and trade stories around the lunch table, and he knew he could never join them. He was certain they would look at him differently if they knew what had happened. Worse, he believed that someone stronger, someone smarter, would never have been taken in the first place. He had walked into that situation, after all—he had accepted the assignment—so the humiliation was his to carry.

The moment that finally pushed him to seek help came on a Tuesday afternoon. He was clearing a fallen branch from a trail when a mountain biker rounded a bend too fast, nearly colliding with him. Rohan dropped the branch, threw himself sideways into a bush, and let out a yell that startled both of them. The biker apologized profusely, but Rohan could not stop shaking. He sat on the ground for ten minutes, his ribs aching from no blow. That evening, he told Sarah he needed to talk to someone. He did not know if talking would help—he had never believed that safety was possible, no matter what anyone said—but he was tired of living inside the snapshots, and even more tired of the terror of being seen falling apart. Lately, even a casual mention of military service from a visitor at the front desk made his stomach drop, and the sight of a uniformed park volunteer made him want to turn around and walk back into the woods. He could not keep running forever.
